## Simple explanation

A graphics processing unit (GPU) is a processor with many parallel
computing units. GPUs can accelerate machine-learning operations that
perform similar calculations across large arrays of data.

## Technical explanation

GPUs execute many threads and are optimized for throughput on parallel
workloads. AI frameworks use GPU kernels for operations such as matrix
multiplication and convolution. Performance depends on hardware,
memory bandwidth, kernel implementation, batch size, software stack,
and data-transfer overhead.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

GPUs can make model training and inference practical for workloads that
would be too slow on general-purpose CPUs. Their memory capacity,
availability, cost, power use, and compatibility influence architecture
and deployment decisions.

## How it works

Data and model parameters are placed in GPU-accessible memory. Parallel
kernels perform operations across many elements, often asynchronously
with the CPU. Frameworks manage execution details, but transfers and
synchronization can affect performance.

## Practical example

A deep-learning framework can run a batch of image convolutions on a
GPU, processing many pixels and channels in parallel.

## Common misconceptions

- A GPU does not accelerate every workload; small or sequential tasks
  may run faster on a CPU.
- GPU performance depends on memory and data pipelines as well as raw
  compute.
- CUDA refers to NVIDIA's GPU computing platform, not to all GPUs.
